# 2 Corinthians 5 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## v. 1 — The Earthly Tent and the Eternal Building

**Traditional Reading:** Paul contrasts our present mortal body ("earthly tent") with the future resurrection body ("building from God"). The word "for" ties this back to 4:16-18 — the outer man is decaying, but that is not the end. "Tent" (*skēnos*) pictures a temporary, movable dwelling; Paul was a tentmaker by trade (Acts 18:3) and uses his trade metaphor. "Torn down" (*kataluō*) is the word for striking a tent. The "building from God, not made with hands" is the glorified resurrection body, not a heavenly mansion (though some older commentaries take it as heaven itself). Jesus used the same phrase "not made with hands" for His own resurrection body (Mark 14:58). Paul says "we know" (*eidō*) — intuitive, Spirit-given certainty, not mere hope. The present tense "we have" indicates the promise is so certain that it is spoken of as already possessed.

— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-5/ ; https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-corinthians-5-commentary

**Gill (Baptist, 18th century):** Notes the body is called a "house" and "tabernacle" — the soul's dwelling. The "if" is a concession: "though" the earthly house be dissolved. The "building of God" includes both the intermediate state glory and the resurrection body. Gill also points out Jewish parallels: rabbis spoke of "the house of the body" and "the tabernacle of the soul."

— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_corinthians/5.htm

**Ellicott:** Notes Paul fuses metaphors of tent and garment. "Clothed upon" reflects Paul's expectation that the Lord's coming might be near; he wishes to be changed without dying (cf. 1 Cor 15:51; 1 Thess 4:15).

— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_corinthians/5.htm

**Denominational note — Baptist (Spurgeon):** "Many people are in a great fright about the future, yet here is Paul viewing the worst thing that could happen to him with such complacency that he likens it to nothing worse than the pulling down of a tent." Spurgeon emphasizes that our future body is so glorious that the dissolution of this one is no loss.

— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-5/

---

## v. 2 — Groaning and Longing to Be Clothed

**Traditional Reading:** Believers "groan" not merely from suffering but from a Spirit-wrought yearning for the heavenly body. The same groaning is in Romans 8:23 — "we groan inwardly as we wait eagerly for our adoption as sons, the redemption of our bodies." Paul desires to be "clothed upon" (to put on the resurrection body like a garment over the present one) rather than to be "unclothed" (a bodiless spirit, which was the Greek philosophical ideal but Paul saw as undesirable).

— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-5/ ; https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-corinthians-5-commentary

**Ellicott:** The phrase "clothed upon" (*ependysasthai*) means putting on a garment over the existing one. Paul hoped to live until Christ's return and be transformed without experiencing death — the incorruptible body superimposed on the corruptible.

— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_corinthians/5.htm

---

## v. 3 — Not Found Naked

**Traditional Reading:** "Naked" means bodiless — a state Paul does not desire. The Greek philosophers (Platonists, Gnostics) considered the body a prison and a bodiless spirit the highest existence. Paul counters this: God created the body good, and the resurrection body is the goal. Being "clothed" means possessing a glorified body, not floating as a disembodied soul.

— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-5/

**Gill:** Sees the "clothing" as both the robe of Christ's righteousness now and the heavenly glory to come. Those clothed with Christ's righteousness will not be found naked at the judgment. He also notes a Jewish Zohar tradition about souls being "clothed with that other body which is in paradise."

— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_corinthians/5.htm

---

## v. 4 — Burdened, Not Wanting to Be Unclothed

**Traditional Reading:** Paul clarifies he does not desire death for its own sake ("not that we would be unclothed"). The natural human recoil from death is acknowledged. Instead he desires to be "further clothed" — to have mortality "swallowed up by life." He would prefer to be alive at Christ's return and transformed instantly (1 Cor 15:51-54) rather than pass through death. The groaning is partly from the burdens of this life — sin, affliction, the body's frailty — but the greater longing is for immortal life.

— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-5/ ; https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-corinthians-5-commentary

**Enduring Word (Pentecostal/Charismatic):** David Guzik notes that in medieval times some Christians were buried in monks' clothing, hoping to improve their standing at the judgment. Paul says Jesus offers a far better garment — the resurrection body itself.

— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-5/

---

## v. 5 — God's Preparation and the Spirit as Pledge

**Traditional Reading:** The same God who "prepared us for this very purpose" (glorification) has given the Spirit as a "pledge" or "guarantee" (*arrhabōn*). This Greek word is a commercial term for a down payment that secures the full purchase and gives legal claim to the goods. In modern Greek, *arrhabōna* means "engagement ring." The Holy Spirit in the believer's life is the foretaste and guarantee of the full inheritance. The preparation God does now (including through afflictions — 2 Cor 4:17) is shaping us to "fit in up there."

— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-5/ ; https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-corinthians-5-commentary

**Spurgeon (Baptist):** "The Holy Spirit is a part of heaven itself. The work of the Holy Spirit in the soul is the bud of heaven. Grace will not be withdrawn… but will be matured into glory."

— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-5/

---

## v. 6 — At Home in the Body, Away from the Lord

**Traditional Reading:** "Always confident" — Paul's confidence rests on God's preparation and the Spirit's pledge. Yet while we live in these bodies, we are "away from the Lord" in the sense of His immediate, visible, glorious presence. This is not ontological absence (God is omnipresent and indwells believers) but the "already/not yet" tension of the Christian life.

— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-5/ ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_corinthians/5.htm

---

## v. 7 — Walk by Faith, Not by Sight

**Traditional Reading:** One of the best-known verses in the NT. "Walk" (*peripateō*) is a Hebrew metaphor for daily conduct and lifestyle. Faith is not a one-time decision but a continuous mode of living. "Not by sight" refers not merely to physical eyes but to living by visible, tangible realities rather than unseen eternal ones (cf. 2 Cor 4:18). Spurgeon noted that walking is a mundane activity — the test of faith is not just in great spiritual moments but in daily, ordinary tasks: "Can you cook a dinner by faith?"

— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-5/ ; https://www.preceptaustin.org/2corinthians_56-8_commentary

**Bible.org (Evangelical):** Notes this is a recurrent NT theme (cf. 4:18; Heb 11:1, 10, 27; 1 Pet 1:8). Believers live in the physical realm but by faith trust in the invisible realm.

— https://new.bible.org/seriespage/2-corinthians-5

---

## v. 8 — Absent from the Body, Present with the Lord

**Traditional Reading:** Paul would "prefer" to depart and be with Christ. This verse is a key proof text against two doctrines: (1) **soul sleep** — the idea that believers enter unconscious suspension until the resurrection. Paul says to be absent from the body *is* to be present with the Lord, not in an unconscious state. (2) **purgatory** — the idea that believers must undergo post-death purification through suffering. Paul expects to be immediately with Christ upon death. "Present with the Lord" is what makes heaven heaven — more than reunion with loved ones or streets of gold.

— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-5/

**Denominational note — Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word):** Guzik notes the question of an intermediate state: are believers bodiless until the resurrection? Paul's use of "unclothed" as undesirable (v. 4) suggests either (a) the dead in Christ are with the Lord in a temporary spiritual body awaiting the final resurrection, or (b) because of the nature of timeless eternity, they already possess their resurrection bodies in the eternal "now."

— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-5/

**Gill:** Says the interval between death and resurrection is a state of absence from the body, during which the soul exists in a separate state — not inactive or sleeping, but in happiness and glory.

— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_corinthians/5.htm

---

## v. 9 — Our Aim: Please Him

**Traditional Reading:** Since we will spend eternity with the Lord, our present ambition (*philotimeomai* — to make it one's honour, to aspire earnestly) should be to please Him. This is Pauline ambition redirected from self-glory to God-pleasing. Whether we are still in the body or already with the Lord, the aim is the same. But there are ways of pleasing God available *only* while we are in the body: exercising faith, enduring trials, sharing the gospel, showing courage — these opportunities cease at death.

— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-5/

---

## v. 10 — The Judgment Seat of Christ

**Traditional Reading (Evangelical consensus):** The "judgment seat" (*bēma*) was the raised platform where a Roman magistrate sat to render judicial decisions and award prizes at athletic games. In Corinth, the *bēma* was a well-known public structure. This is **not** the Great White Throne judgment of Revelation 20:11-15 (the judgment of the unsaved). This is the judgment of **believers' works**, not determination of eternal destiny. Salvation is secure; rewards are at stake. Both deeds and motives will be evaluated. As in 1 Corinthians 3:12-15, works will be tested by fire — what was done for Christ remains; what was done in the flesh is burned up. The believer "suffers loss" (of reward) but is "saved, yet so as through fire."

— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-5/ ; https://www.preceptaustin.org/2corinthians_510_commentary

**Key detail:** The word for "bad" is *phaulos* ("worthless, useless") rather than *ponēros* ("evil, wicked"). This supports the interpretation that it is about worthless deeds being discarded, not sins being punished (since Christ bore sin's penalty). The believer may forfeit reward but not salvation.

— https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-corinthians/5-10.html

**Gill (Baptist):** Everyone — ministers and people, all ranks — must appear. Good works are rewarded by grace, not merit. They serve as "fruits of grace and evidences of the truth of faith" which justify the Judge in His verdict. Evil works receive strict proportional recompense.

— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_corinthians/5.htm

**Denominational differences — Judgment Seat:** Some traditions (especially those emphasizing final perseverance) see the *bēma* as a positive evaluation of believers only, with no punitive aspect. Others (some Reformed) see it as including a real, sober accountability that should produce "fear of the Lord" (v. 11). The Catholic and Orthodox traditions place this in the context of the particular judgment at death and the final judgment at Christ's return, where works done in grace merit reward (see Catholic note at v. 21 below). The majority Protestant view, however, distinguishes this from the final judgment of the unsaved and sees it as an assessment for rewards, not condemnation (Rom 8:1).

— https://www.preceptaustin.org/2corinthians_510_commentary

---

## v. 11 — The Fear of the Lord and Persuading Men

**Traditional Reading:** "Knowing the fear of the Lord" connects to v. 10 — reverence and awe before the Judge motivates evangelism. "We persuade men" means gospel preaching is an act of persuasion, not mere information-sharing. Paul wanted to convince people to come to Christ. "We are made manifest to God" — God already knows Paul's heart; he doesn't need to persuade God. He hopes the Corinthians' consciences also recognize his integrity.

— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-5/

**Bible.org:** The phrase "fear of the Lord" relates directly to the judgment seat in v. 10. There is a respect and awe (Acts 5:11; 9:31) due the Judge of the universe (Heb 10:31; 12:29). Believers are motivated both to godly living and to sharing the gospel by the knowledge that each will give an account.

— https://new.bible.org/seriespage/2-corinthians-5

---

## v. 12 — Not Self-Commendation but Defense

**Traditional Reading:** Paul is not boasting. He is giving the Corinthians ammunition to answer his critics — the "false teachers" who "boast in appearance and not in heart." The Corinthian culture valued rhetorical polish, impressive presence, and status. Paul's sufferings made him look weak; his critics looked impressive by worldly standards. Paul wants the Corinthians to value the heart, not appearance (cf. 1 Sam 16:7).

— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-5/

---

## v. 13 — Beside Ourselves or of Sound Mind

**Traditional Reading:** Paul's critics said he was crazy. Festus would later say, "Paul, you are out of your mind!" (Acts 26:24). Jesus was also accused of being insane (Mark 3:21). Paul's response: if he seems crazy, it is for God's sake — his radical devotion looks irrational to the world. If he is in his right mind, it is for their benefit. Either way, his ministry is authentic.

— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-5/

---

## vv. 14-15 — The Love of Christ Compels / One Died for All

**Traditional Reading:** Christ's love is the driving force behind Paul's ministry. "Compels" (*synechō*) means to press on, constrain, or hem in — Paul is carried along by Christ's love, not his own ambition. "One died for all, therefore all died": Christ's death was substitutionary and representative. When Christ died, those He represented died with Him (cf. Rom 6:3-8; Gal 2:20). The purpose: "that those who live should no longer live for themselves but for Him who died for them and was raised."

— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-5/

**Denominational note — Reformed / Particular Redemption:** Some Calvinists read "all died" as "all the elect died" — Christ died for all without distinction (Jew and Gentile) but particularly for the elect. Others read it as universal in extent — Christ died for every person.

**Denominational note — Arminian/Wesleyan:** Typically read "all" as genuinely universal — Christ died for every human being, and the "all died" means all are potentially included in His death; those who live by faith then experience that death to self.

— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-5/

---

## v. 16 — Regarding No One According to the Flesh

**Traditional Reading:** Since we are new creations in Christ, we no longer evaluate people by worldly standards — ethnicity, social status, wealth, education. "Even though we have known Christ according to the flesh" likely refers either to (a) a pre-conversion, merely human estimation of Jesus as a Jewish teacher or political messiah — Paul formerly thought this way but no longer does; or (b) Paul having known the historical Jesus during His earthly ministry (less likely, as Paul was not among Jesus' earthly disciples). The new creation perspective transforms how we see everyone.

— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-5/

**Gill:** Sees this as Paul saying he no longer regards men on account of carnal descent or outward privileges (as Jews did), nor Christ in a carnal view as a temporal king.

— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_corinthians/5.htm

---

## v. 17 — New Creation

**Traditional Reading:** One of the most celebrated verses in Paul. "In Christ" denotes union with Him. "New creation" (*kainē ktisis*) — not just a repaired old life, but something genuinely new. "The old has passed away" — the old covenant era, old way of living, old identity in Adam. "The new has come." This is both individual (each believer is a new creation) and corporate (the church as the new humanity).

— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-5/

**Denominational note — Reformed:** Emphasizes that "in Christ" union is the ground of all salvation blessings. The new creation is forensic (new status) as well as transformative (new nature). This verse undergirds the doctrine of regeneration.

**Denominational note — Wesleyan/Methodist:** Emphasizes that the new creation involves actual transformation of the heart — holiness of life, not just imputed status. The old has truly passed away in experience, not just position.

**Denominational note — Catholic/Orthodox:** The Orthodox especially see "new creation" in cosmic and sacramental terms — in Christ the whole cosmos is being renewed, and the believer participates in this through baptism, the Eucharist, and the life of the Church. The "new creation" is both already inaugurated and not yet complete (theosis).

---

## vv. 18-19 — The Ministry of Reconciliation

**Traditional Reading:** "All this is from God" — the entire work of new creation and reconciliation originates in God, not human effort. God "reconciled us to Himself through Christ" — reconciliation implies a prior estrangement (sin) that God bridges. The initiative is entirely His. God has given believers "the ministry of reconciliation" — the commission to carry His reconciling message to the world. Verse 19 elaborates: "God was in Christ reconciling the world to Himself, not counting men's trespasses against them." This is the heart of the gospel: sin is not imputed to those who are in Christ.

— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-5/

---

## v. 20 — Ambassadors for Christ

**Traditional Reading:** An ambassador represents a sovereign and speaks on his behalf. Believers are Christ's ambassadors, making His appeal to a rebellious world. "As though God were making His appeal through us" — the astonishing dignity and responsibility of gospel proclamation: when the gospel is faithfully preached, it is God Himself who appeals. "We implore you on behalf of Christ: Be reconciled to God." Though the work of reconciliation is accomplished by Christ, the command to be reconciled implies human response — people must receive the reconciliation God offers.

— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-5/

---

## v. 21 — The Great Exchange

This is one of the most theologically freighted verses in the NT, and traditions differ markedly.

**Reformed / Classic Protestant Reading (Imputed Righteousness):** This verse teaches "double imputation." God "made Him who knew no sin to be sin" — by judicial imputation, our sin was credited to Christ, and He bore its penalty on the cross. He did not become sinful in His nature; He was *treated as sin* in a forensic, legal sense. "So that in Him we might become the righteousness of God" — by the same mechanism of imputation, Christ's perfect righteousness is credited to believers. This is "alien righteousness" (Luther): a righteousness from outside ourselves, received by faith alone. Christ takes our sin; we receive His righteousness. This verse is the classic proof text for the Protestant doctrine of justification by faith alone through the imputed righteousness of Christ.

— https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/faith-and-the-imputation-of-righteousness ; https://www.gty.org/blogs/B210217/the-word-of-reconciliation ; https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/essay/the-doctrine-of-justification/

**Piper (Desiring God, Baptist/Reformed):** "Here we have a double imputation. God imputed our sins to Christ who knew no sin. And God imputed his righteousness to us who had no righteousness of our own." Faith is what unites us to Christ, not what makes us righteous.

— https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/faith-and-the-imputation-of-righteousness

**MacArthur (GTY, Baptist):** "Christ was 'made… to be sin' by imputation… The legal obligation stemming from sin's guilt was transferred to Christ, and He bore its full penalty." Christ "stood as a proxy for His people at the bar of divine justice."

— https://www.gty.org/blogs/B210217/the-word-of-reconciliation

**Wesleyan/Methodist View:** Agrees that Christ's righteousness is the sole ground of acceptance with God, but tends to emphasize that "becoming the righteousness of God" also involves actual moral transformation. The righteousness is imputed AND imparted — received by faith but also worked out in holy living. Some Wesleyans are cautious about the phrase "imputed righteousness" if it is taken to mean that no actual change occurs in the believer.

**Catholic View:** The Council of Trent (Session 6, Chapter 7) taught that justification is not merely remission of sins but "sanctification and renewal of the inward man." The righteousness received is not merely imputed but is a real, inherent righteousness infused by the Holy Spirit. 2 Corinthians 5:21 is understood as Christ becoming a sin offering (a sacrificial victim), not literally "sin" in the abstract. The believer becomes truly righteous through the grace of Christ, not merely declared righteous while remaining internally unchanged. The Catholic Catechism (CCC 602) cites this verse in discussing Christ's substitutionary role as the Suffering Servant.

— https://www.newadvent.org (search "Trent justification"); https://www.catholic.com

**Orthodox View:** The Orthodox emphasize *theosis* (deification): "that we might become the righteousness of God" is understood as genuine participation in God's uncreated energies and righteousness — not merely a legal status but transformation into Christ's likeness. The concept of "imputed righteousness" as a purely forensic declaration is generally rejected as too legalistic, though Orthodox do affirm that we are saved by Christ's work, not our own merit.

— https://www.oca.org

**Modern Scholarly Note:** The NET Bible notes point out that "made Him… to be sin" may reflect the Hebrew idiom for a sin offering (*ḥaṭṭā't*), meaning "God made Him a sin offering for us." This would connect the verse to the Suffering Servant of Isaiah 53.

— https://netbible.org

**Hyper-Grace / Word of Faith Views:** Some modern popular teachers in the Word of Faith or hyper-grace streams teach that in this exchange, Christ literally became sinful in nature on the cross — that He took on a satanic nature and had to be "born again" in hell. This goes well beyond imputation. Mainstream traditions (Protestant, Catholic, Orthodox) universally reject this as heretical, insisting Christ remained personally sinless and holy even while bearing sin's penalty.

---

## Summary of Key Inter-Tradition Differences in This Chapter

| Verse | Issue | Reformed/Baptist | Wesleyan/Methodist | Catholic/Orthodox |
|-------|-------|------------------|-------------------|-------------------|
| **v. 10** | Judgment Seat | Believers' rewards only; sins already paid | Believers' works evaluated; sober accountability | Part of particular & final judgment; works done in grace merit |
| **v. 17** | New Creation | Primarily forensic + transformative | Emphasises actual heart transformation | Cosmic renewal; sacramental participation; theosis |
| **v. 21** | Righteousness | Imputed (alien) righteousness; forensic | Imputed + imparted; actual holiness included | Infused (inherent) righteousness; real transformation |
